metadata.title: The Fourth Gate
metadata.series_position: episode 14 — a sign-off that documents its own weaknesses, and a fourth gate nobody named
metadata.note: cli-explainer spine, weekly work report, claude-hai channel. Episode 14, from the last pushed commit on chore/promote-scenariostresstestingagent (20795b2; origin contains it). FRAMEWORK: CAN IT FAIL / WHAT HAPPENS TO A FAILURE IT CANNOT JUDGE / WHAT WAS WRITTEN DOWN UNASKED. Hero is B05: gates 1, 3 and 6 reproduced standalone against planted defects. B06 is an ORIGINAL FINDING not in the commit — gate 4's fallback greps for '[TODO: DEV]', a string that appears inside gate 4's own test command in the file being searched, so it can never fail. B07 CORRECTS THE COMMIT MESSAGE: it groups gate 6 with 'cannot fail', but gate 6 measured exit 1 — it cannot pass, which is the opposite defect with the opposite consequence.

render.note: 4K-native sources: Manim at 2160p24, Remotion at scale 2.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — composer, ask lands answered. Speaks the author's name.
beats.narration_text: I'm Uday Sonawane, and this is my week on Mycroft. I signed off a promotion: one recipe moved from draft to runnable-sample. The sign-off lists three of its own gates that cannot fail. Recounting it, I found a fourth that nobody had named.
beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the week's ask, answered

shot.show: the Claude composer with the week's ask and its three-line answer

props.command: claude "I'm signing this promotion off — what is wrong with the evidence?"
output: three gates cannot fail as written
a fourth has the same defect, unnamed
and one of the three is the opposite bug

beats.role_note: the premise — a promotion that documents its own weaknesses
beats.narration_text: Here is what happened. One recipe moved one step along the lifecycle — draft to runnable-sample — and only two lines of it changed: the status, and a pointer to the evidence. Live execution stays blocked. What makes it worth an episode is the sign-off itself, which lists, in writing, the ways its own evidence is weak. Three gate tests that cannot fail. Four steps that read a fixture folder instead of the previous step's output. Nobody made the signer write that down.
beats.new_visual_element: the promotion, and the weaknesses attached to it

shot.show: DRAFT to RUNNABLE-SAMPLE, two lines changed, with the self-reported weaknesses beside it
shot.visual_intent: Left, a bordered card: DRAFT with an arrow to RUNNABLE-SAMPLE, and beneath it 'status and last_gate — two lines'. Right, in terracotta, a panel headed 'what the sign-off says about itself' listing three gates that cannot fail and steps 3-6 reading fixtures. A chip below: live execution still blocked.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — three questions, AS A STRUCTURE before the evidence
beats.narration_text: Three questions for any check that guards anything. One: can it fail — not in theory, but when you run it against something you broke on purpose. Two: what happens to a failure it cannot judge — because a check that discards what it cannot classify will report a clean run forever. Three: what did the signer write down that nobody required them to write down.
beats.new_visual_element: the three questions, as a numbered structure

shot.show: three numbered cards: CAN IT FAIL / WHAT HAPPENS TO A FAILURE IT CANNOT JUDGE / WHAT WAS WRITTEN DOWN UNASKED
shot.visual_intent: Three bordered cards land in a row, one per narration step. The first lands in terracotta — it is the one this episode is built on — and the reel is scored against all three.

beats.narration_text: The ask was to take my own sign-off apart before anyone else did.

shot.show: the composer with the audit ask

props.command: claude "run every gate test against something broken — which ones still pass?"
props.segment: The ask · break them on purpose
output: run each gate against a planted defect
report what cannot fail, and why

beats.role_note: ACTUAL-CODE LAW — the three gate tests, verbatim from the committed recipe
beats.narration_text: These are the three, verbatim. Gate one ends in or-true. Gate three runs a JSON parser through find's exec. Gate six tests for a file whose name still contains the literal placeholder, square-bracket DATE.

props.title: recipes/scenariostresstestingagent.md @ 20795b2 — three gate tests
props.code:
# gate 1 — source gate
test -f "recipes/<recipe>.md" \
  && rg -n "\\[TODO: DEFINE]" "recipes/<recipe>.md" || true
#                                                        ^^^^^^^

# gate 3 — data-shape gate
find data/raw/<recipe> data/verified/<recipe> -name "*.json" \
  -print -exec python3 -m json.tool {} \;
#        ^^^^^ find's exit code ignores what -exec returns

# gate 6 — report gate
test -f logs/<recipe>-[DATE].json \
  && test -f reports/generated/<recipe>-[DATE].md
#                              ^^^^^^ a literal placeholder
props.sparkLine: Three tests. None of them tests anything.

beats.role_note: HERO BEAT — all three reproduced standalone, with a result the commit did not predict
beats.narration_text: I ran all three outside the repository, on files I broke on purpose. Gate one returns zero every time — when the pattern is there, when it is absent, and, which surprised me, when the file it checks does not exist at all. Gate three: find reports success even though the JSON parser it invoked exited one on the broken file. The failure is real, and find swallows it. Gate six does something different. It returns one. Every time.
beats.new_visual_element: the three gates, run against planted defects

shot.show: gate 1 exit 0 in three cases; gate 3 swallows a real failure; gate 6 exits 1
shot.visual_intent: Three bordered panels stacked, each with its real exit codes. Panels one and two in soft ink, each showing exit 0 beside a defect that should have failed it. Panel three, in terracotta, shows exit equals one. Citation strip: all three reproduced standalone, outside the repo.

beats.role_note: the fourth gate — a finding of my own, not in the commit
beats.narration_text: Then the one nobody named. Gate four says: the step script exists, or there is a typed development to-do. So if the script is missing, it searches the recipe for the string to-do colon D-E-V. And that string is in the recipe — it is sitting inside gate four's own test command, which is written in the file being searched. The gate greps for itself. I reproduced it with the script deleted and every real to-do removed: it still passes, on the strength of its own definition.
beats.new_visual_element: gate 4 matching its own test command

shot.show: the gate's pattern lives in the file the gate searches
shot.visual_intent: A single wide bordered panel holding gate 4's test line, with the substring TODO: DEV highlighted in terracotta inside the command itself. An arrow curves from that highlighted substring back to the filename at the end of the same line. Beneath, a terracotta chip: script deleted, all real TODOs removed, still exits 0.

beats.role_note: the recount — including a correction to my own commit message
beats.narration_text: The recount, and this time it corrects me. The commit groups gates one, three and six together as, quote, cannot fail as written. One and three, yes. But gate six is the opposite defect: there is no file named with a literal placeholder, so it cannot ever pass. Those are not the same bug, and the difference matters — a gate stuck on pass hides problems quietly forever, while a gate stuck on fail gets noticed the first time somebody runs it. Two more. The parity check is twenty-four of twenty-four matching, but there are twenty-five rows; one was not modelled. And the run log says one self-test was skipped, where the committed result file records zero — different runs, on different machines.
beats.new_visual_element: what reproduced, and the three corrections

shot.show: gate 6 is cannot-pass not cannot-fail; parity 24 of 25 rows; skipped 1 vs 0
shot.visual_intent: Top: a terracotta panel contrasting 'the commit says: cannot fail' against 'gate 6 measured: exit 1 — cannot pass', with a one-line consequence beneath. Below, two soft-ink rows with hollow boxes: parity 24 of 25 rows, one not modelled; skipped 1 in the log, 0 in the artifact. Citation strip.

beats.role_note: what did hold up — every figure recounted independently
beats.narration_text: What survived the recount, and most of it did. The clean corpus: twelve records in, twelve accepted, none rejected. The defective corpus: ten planted defects, ten rejected, none accepted. Both runs declare sample mode, so nothing went live. The self-tests read twenty-seven of twenty-seven, thirty-one of thirty-one, and thirty-seven of thirty-seven in the committed artifacts. And the lifecycle counts land exactly: ninety-four drafts, three runnable-samples, ninety-seven recipes. There are ninety-nine markdown files in that folder — the other two are a README and a shared include, and they are not recipes.

shot.show: 12 in 12 accepted, 10 planted 10 rejected, self-tests, and 94+3=97 of 99 files
shot.visual_intent: A bordered panel of ticked rows, each a recounted figure with its source: the two corpora, the three self-test totals, and the lifecycle count. The final row, in terracotta, reads '99 .md files — 2 are not recipes' with a tick, because that one needed checking.

beats.role_note: the discipline — what a good sign-off looks like even when the evidence is weak
beats.narration_text: So why sign it at all. Because the promotion is honest about its own limits, and it leaves the repository in a better state than it found it. Live execution stays blocked — there is no approval record, and the status does not pretend otherwise. The recipe version stays at zero-point-four-point-zero, so the evidence binds to the exact text that was reviewed. And the next action in the handoff used to say promote this recipe. It now says: make its gate tests real. The promotion did not close an item. It opened a better one.
beats.new_visual_element: the three things the sign-off did right

shot.show: live blocked, version frozen, and the open item it replaced itself with
shot.visual_intent: Three bordered rows with ticks: 'live blocked — no approval record', 'recipe_version frozen at 0.4.0 — evidence binds to the reviewed text', and a terracotta row showing the handoff line struck through, 'promote this recipe', replaced by 'make its gate tests real'.

beats.role_note: scaffolded task — the rubric on the viewer's own checks, with a GOOD/BAD discriminator
beats.narration_text: Your turn, and it takes about five minutes. Take any check that guards your pipeline. Break the thing it is supposed to catch, then run it. If it still passes, you have learned what that check has been telling you all year.
